{{short description|Algebraic equation on which the solution of a differential equation depends}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''characteristic equation''' (or '''auxiliary equation'''<ref name="edwards" />) is an [[algebraic equation]] of [[degree of a polynomial|degree]] {{mvar|n}} upon which depends the solution of a given {{nowrap begin}}{{mvar|n}}th-{{nowrap end}}[[Differential equation#Equation order|order]] [[differential equation]]<ref name="smith">{{cite web|url=http://etc.usf.edu/lit2go/contents/2800/2892/2892_txt.html|title=History of Modern Mathematics: Differential Equations|last=Smith|first=David Eugene|publisher=[[University of South Florida]]}}</ref> or [[linear difference equation|difference equation]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Baumol|first=William J.|title=Economic Dynamics|url=https://archive.org/details/economicdynamics0000baum_c7i2|url-access=registration|edition=3rd|date=1970|page=[https://archive.org/details/economicdynamics0000baum_c7i2/page/172 172]}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Chiang|first=Alpha|title=Fundamental Methods of Mathematical Economics|url=https://archive.org/details/fundamentalmetho0000chia_h4v2|url-access=registration|edition=3rd|date=1984|pages=[https://archive.org/details/fundamentalmetho0000chia_h4v2/page/578 578], 600|publisher=McGraw-Hill |isbn=9780070107809 }}</ref> The characteristic equation can only be formed when the differential equation is [[linear differential equation|linear]] and [[Homogeneous differential equation#Homogeneous linear differential equations|homogeneous]], and has constant [[coefficient]]s.<ref name="edwards">{{cite book|last1=Edwards |first1=C. Henry |last2=Penney |first2=David E. |others=David Calvis |title=Differential Equations: Computing and Modeling |publisher=Pearson Education |location=[[Upper Saddle River]], [[New Jersey]] |pages=156–170 |chapter=Chapter 3 |year=2008 |isbn=978-0-13-600438-7}}</ref>  Such a differential equation, with {{mvar|y}} as the [[dependent variable]], superscript {{math|(''n'')}} denoting ''n''<sup>th</sup>-[[derivative]], and {{math|''a''<sub>''n''</sub>, ''a''<sub>''n'' − 1</sub>, ..., ''a''<sub>1</sub>, ''a''<sub>0</sub>}} as constants,
:<math>a_{n}y^{(n)} + a_{n-1}y^{(n-1)} + \cdots + a_{1}y' + a_{0}y = 0,</math>
will have a characteristic equation of the form
:<math>a_{n}r^{n} + a_{n-1}r^{n-1} + \cdots + a_{1}r + a_{0} = 0</math>
whose solutions {{math|''r''<sub>1</sub>, ''r''<sub>2</sub>, ..., ''r''<sub>''n''</sub>}} are the roots from which the [[general solution]] can be formed.<ref name="edwards" /><ref name=eFunda>{{cite web |url=http://www.efunda.com/math/ode/linearode_consthomo.cfm |title=Linear Homogeneous Ordinary Differential Equations with Constant Coefficients |last1=Chu |first1=Herman |last2=Shah |first2=Gaurav |last3=Macall |first3=Tom |publisher=eFunda |accessdate=1 March 2011}}</ref><ref name="cohen">{{cite book|last=Cohen|first=Abraham|title=An Elementary Treatise on Differential Equations|url=https://archive.org/details/anelementarytre01cohegoog|publisher=[[D. C. Heath and Company]]|year=1906}}</ref>  Analogously, a linear difference equation of the form

:<math>y_{t+n} = b_1y_{t+n-1} + \cdots + b_ny_{t}</math>

has characteristic equation

:<math>r^n - b_1r^{n-1} - \cdots - b_n =0,</math>

discussed in more detail at [[Linear recurrence with constant coefficients]].

The characteristic roots ([[root of a polynomial|roots]] of the characteristic equation) also provide qualitative information about the behavior of the variable whose evolution is described by the dynamic equation. For a differential equation parameterized on time, the variable's evolution is [[Lyapunov stability|stable]] [[if and only if]] the [[real part]] of each root is negative. For difference equations, there is stability if and only if the [[Complex number#Polar complex plane|modulus]] of each root is less than 1. For both types of equation, persistent fluctuations occur if there is at least one pair of [[complex number|complex]] roots.

The method of [[Integral|integrating]] linear [[ordinary differential equation]]s with constant coefficients was discovered by [[Leonhard Euler]], who found that the solutions depended on an algebraic 'characteristic' equation.<ref name="smith" />  The qualities of the Euler's characteristic equation were later considered in greater detail by French mathematicians [[Augustin-Louis Cauchy]] and [[Gaspard Monge]].<ref name="smith" /><ref name="cohen" />

==  Derivation ==

Starting with a linear homogeneous differential equation with constant coefficients {{math|''a''<sub>''n''</sub>, ''a''<sub>''n'' − 1</sub>, ..., ''a''<sub>1</sub>, ''a''<sub>0</sub>}},
:<math>a_n y^{(n)} + a_{n-1}y^{(n-1)} + \cdots + a_1 y^\prime + a_0 y = 0,</math>
it can be seen that if {{math|''y''(''x'') {{=}} ''e''<sup>{{hairsp}}''rx''</sup>}}, each term would be a constant multiple of {{math|''e''<sup>{{hairsp}}''rx''</sup>}}.  This results from the fact that the derivative of the [[exponential function]] {{math|''e''<sup>{{hairsp}}''rx''</sup>}} is a multiple of itself.  Therefore, {{math|''y''′ {{=}} ''re''<sup>{{hairsp}}''rx''</sup>}}, {{math|1=''y''″ = ''r''<sup>2</sup>''e''<sup>{{hairsp}}''rx''</sup>}}, and {{math|1=''y''<sup>(''n'')</sup> = ''r''<sup>''n''</sup>''e''<sup>{{hairsp}}''rx''</sup>}} are all multiples.  This suggests that certain values of {{mvar|r}} will allow multiples of {{math|''e''<sup>{{hairsp}}''rx''</sup>}} to sum to zero, thus solving the homogeneous differential equation.<ref name="eFunda" />  In order to solve for {{mvar|r}}, one can substitute {{math|1=''y'' = ''e''<sup>{{hairsp}}''rx''</sup>}} and its derivatives into the differential equation to get
:<math>a_n r^n e^{rx} + a_{n-1}r^{n-1}e^{rx} + \cdots + a_1 re^{rx} + a_0 e^{rx} = 0</math>
Since {{math|''e''<sup>{{hairsp}}''rx''</sup>}} can never equal zero, it can be divided out, giving the characteristic equation
:<math>a_n r^n + a_{n-1}r^{n-1} + \cdots + a_1 r + a_0 = 0.</math>
By solving for the roots, {{mvar|r}}, in this characteristic equation, one can find the general solution to the differential equation.<ref name="edwards" /><ref name="cohen" />  For example, if {{mvar|r}} has roots equal to 3, 11, and 40, then the general solution will be <math>y(x) = c_1 e^{3 x} + c_2 e^{11 x} + c_3 e^{40 x}</math>, where <math>c_1</math>, <math>c_2</math>, and <math>c_3</math>  are [[Constant of integration|arbitrary constants]] which need to be determined by the boundary and/or initial conditions.

== Formation of the general solution ==
Solving the characteristic equation for its roots, {{math|''r''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''r''<sub>''n''</sub>}}, allows one to find the general solution of the differential equation.  The roots may be [[real number|real]] or [[complex number|complex]], as well as distinct or repeated.  If a characteristic equation has parts with distinct real roots, {{mvar|h}} repeated roots, or {{mvar|k}} complex roots corresponding to general solutions of {{math|''y''<sub>D</sub>(''x'')}}, {{math|''y''<sub>R<sub>1</sub></sub>(''x''), ..., ''y''<sub>R<sub>''h''</sub></sub>(''x'')}}, and {{math|''y''<sub>C<sub>1</sub></sub>(''x''), ..., ''y''<sub>C<sub>''k''</sub></sub>(''x'')}}, respectively, then the general solution to the differential equation is
:<math>y(x) = y_\mathrm{D}(x) + y_{\mathrm{R}_1}(x) + \cdots + y_{\mathrm{R}_h}(x) + y_{\mathrm{C}_1}(x) + \cdots + y_{\mathrm{C}_k}(x)</math>

===Example===
The linear homogeneous differential equation with constant coefficients
:<math>y^{(5)} + y^{(4)} - 4y^{(3)} - 16y'' -20y' - 12y = 0</math> 
has the characteristic equation
:<math>r^5 + r^4 - 4r^3 - 16r^2 -20r - 12 = 0</math>
By [[Factorization|factoring]] the characteristic equation into{{explain|reason=How is this factorization found?|date=August 2024}}
:<math>(r - 3)(r^2 + 2r + 2)^2 = 0</math>
one can see that the solutions for {{mvar|r}} are the distinct single root {{math|''r''<sub>1</sub> {{=}} 3}} and the double complex roots {{math|''r''<sub>2,3,4,5</sub> {{=}} 1 ± ''i''}}.  This corresponds to the real-valued general solution
:<math> y(x) = c_1 e^{3x} + e^x(c_2 \cos x + c_3 \sin x) + xe^x(c_4 \cos x + c_5 \sin x)</math>
with constants {{math|''c''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''c''<sub>5</sub>}}.

=== Distinct real roots ===
The ''[[superposition principle]] for linear homogeneous '' says that if {{math|''u''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''u''<sub>''n''</sub>}} are {{mvar|n}} [[linearly independent]] solutions to a particular differential equation, then {{math|''c''<sub>1</sub>''u''<sub>1</sub> + ⋯ + ''c<sub>n</sub>u<sub>n</sub>''}} is also a solution for all values {{math|''c''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''c<sub>n</sub>''}}.<ref name="edwards" /><ref name="dawkins">{{cite web|url=http://tutorial.math.lamar.edu/Classes/DE/PDETerminology.aspx|title=Differential Equation Terminology|last=Dawkins|first=Paul|work=Paul's Online Math Notes|accessdate=2 March 2011}}</ref>  Therefore, if the characteristic equation has distinct real roots {{math|''r''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''r<sub>n</sub>''}}, then a general solution will be of the form
:<math> y_\mathrm{D}(x) = c_1 e^{r_1 x} + c_2 e^{r_2 x} + \cdots + c_n e^{r_n x} </math>

=== Repeated real roots ===
If the characteristic equation has a root {{math|''r''<sub>1</sub>}} that is repeated {{mvar|k}} times, then it is clear that {{math|1=''y''<sub>p</sub>(''x'') = ''c''<sub>1</sub>''e''<sup>{{hairsp}}''r''<sub>1</sub>''x''</sup>}} is at least one solution.<ref name="edwards" />  However, this solution lacks linearly independent solutions from the other {{math|''k'' − 1}} roots.  Since {{math|''r''<sub>1</sub>}} has [[multiplicity (mathematics)|multiplicity]] {{mvar|k}}, the differential equation can be factored into<ref name="edwards" />
:<math>\left ( \frac{d}{dx} - r_1 \right )^k y = 0 .</math>
The fact that {{math|1=''y''<sub>p</sub>(''x'') = ''c''<sub>1</sub>''e''<sup>{{hairsp}}''r''<sub>1</sub>''x''</sup>}} is one solution allows one to presume that the general solution may be of the form {{math|1=''y''(''x'') = ''u''(''x'')''e''<sup>{{hairsp}}''r''<sub>1</sub>''x''</sup>}}, where {{math|''u''(''x'')}} is a function to be determined.  Substituting {{math|''ue''<sup>{{hairsp}}''r''<sub>1</sub>''x''</sup>}} gives
:<math>\left( \frac{d}{dx} - r_1 \right)\! ue^{r_1 x} = \frac{d}{dx}\left(ue^{r_1 x}\right) - r_1 ue^{r_1 x} = \frac{d}{dx}(u)e^{r_1 x} + r_1 ue^{r_1 x}- r_1 ue^{r_1 x} = \frac{d}{dx}(u)e^{r_1 x}</math>
when {{math|1=''k'' = 1}}.  By applying this fact {{mvar|k}} times, it follows that
:<math>\left( \frac{d}{dx} - r_1 \right)^k ue^{r_1 x} = \frac{d^k}{dx^k}(u)e^{r_1 x} = 0.</math>
By dividing out {{math|''e''<sup>{{hairsp}}''r''<sub>1</sub>''x''</sup>}}, it can be seen that
:<math>\frac{d^k}{dx^k}(u) = u^{(k)} = 0.</math>
Therefore, the general case for {{math|''u''(''x'')}} is a [[polynomial]] of degree {{math|''k'' − 1}}, so that {{math|1=''u''(''x'') = ''c''<sub>1</sub> + ''c''<sub>2</sub>''x'' + ''c''<sub>3</sub>''x''<sup>2</sup> + ⋯ + ''c<sub>k</sub>x''<sup>''k''{{hairsp}}−1</sup>}}.<ref name="cohen" />  Since {{math|1=''y''(''x'') = ''ue''<sup>{{hairsp}}''r''<sub>1</sub>''x''</sup>}}, the part of the general solution corresponding to {{math|''r''<sub>1</sub>}} is
:<math>y_\mathrm{R}(x) = e^{r_1 x}\!\left(c_1 + c_2 x + \cdots + c_k x^{k-1}\right).</math>

=== Complex roots ===
If a second-order differential equation has a characteristic equation with [[complex conjugate]] roots of the form {{math|''r''<sub>1</sub> {{=}} ''a'' + ''bi''}} and {{math|''r''<sub>2</sub> {{=}} ''a'' − ''bi''}}, then the general solution is accordingly {{math|''y''(''x'') {{=}} ''c''<sub>1</sub>''e''<sup>(''a'' + ''bi''{{hairsp}})''x''</sup> + ''c''<sub>2</sub>''e''<sup>(''a'' − ''bi''{{hairsp}})''x''</sup>}}.  By [[Euler's formula]], which states that {{math|''e<sup>iθ</sup>'' {{=}} cos(''θ'') + ''i'' sin(''θ'')}}, this solution can be rewritten as follows:
:<math>\begin{align}
y(x) &= c_{1}e^{(a + bi)x} + c_{2}e^{(a - bi)x}\\ 
     &= c_{1}e^{ax}(\cos bx + i \sin bx) + c_{2}e^{ax}( \cos bx - i \sin bx ) \\
     &= \left(c_{1} + c_{2}\right)e^{ax} \cos bx + i(c_{1} - c_{2})e^{ax} \sin bx 
\end{align}</math>
where {{math|''c''<sub>1</sub>}} and {{math|''c''<sub>2</sub>}} are constants that can be non-real and which depend on the initial conditions.<ref name="cohen" /> (Indeed, since {{math|''y''(''x'')}} is real, {{math|''c''<sub>1</sub> − ''c''<sub>2</sub>}} must be [[imaginary number|imaginary]] or zero and {{math|''c''<sub>1</sub> + ''c''<sub>2</sub>}} must be real, in order for both terms after the last [[equals sign]] to be real.)

For example, if {{math|''c''<sub>1</sub> {{=}} ''c''<sub>2</sub> {{=}} {{sfrac|1|2}}}}, then the particular solution {{math|''y''<sub>1</sub>(''x'') {{=}} ''e''<sup>{{hairsp}}''ax''</sup> cos(''bx'')}} is formed. Similarly, if {{math|''c''<sub>1</sub> {{=}} {{sfrac|1|2''i''}}}} and {{math|''c''<sub>2</sub> {{=}} −{{sfrac|1|2''i''}}}}, then the independent solution formed is {{math|''y''<sub>2</sub>(''x'') {{=}} ''e''<sup>{{hairsp}}''ax''</sup> sin(''bx'')}}.  Thus by the ''superposition principle for linear homogeneous differential equations'', a second-order differential equation having complex roots {{math|''r'' {{=}} ''a'' ± ''bi''}} will result in the following general solution:

:<math> y_\mathrm{C}(x) = e^{ax}(C_1 \cos bx + C_2 \sin bx)</math>

This analysis also applies to the parts of the solutions of a higher-order differential equation whose characteristic equation involves non-real complex conjugate roots.
